Both microwave and radio frequency radiation are used to heat materials that are electrically non-conductive and composed of polar molecules. For drying applications, water is the primary polar molecule owing to its partially charged and dipole state. Electromagnetic-based heating is defined by the ability to generate heat in the bulk of the system by causing dipoles in the system, such as water, to align the molecules to an alternating electric field [Altemimi et al 2019, Orsat et al 2005]. This study utilizes an RF system with a 27.12 megahertz (MHz) frequency, which translates to the polarity changing 27.12 million times each second. Additionally, with a changing electric field polarity, the dipoles rotate to align with the field, inducing ohmic heating and frictional dissipation of heat. Here we studied the effects of RF-based drying systems to be used for paper and board drying applications primarily as a function of the moisture content of the paper web. In addition to the details of the experimental setup described earlier, to ensure uniformity during RF application, the sample sled was programmed to oscillate by ±0.51 centimeter (cm) from the central position of Chamber 2 (RF Chamber) at 0.2 m/s. RF was applied during drying both in continuous mode and intermittent mode with only a few pulses in between conventional drying. Figure 8 highlights the instantaneous moisture content as a function of drying time for the 500 watt (W) trial alongside a convection-only trial for ease of comparison. Continuous application of RF results in a significantly faster drying process, with roughly a 53% decrease in the drying 18 DE-EE0009395 time and a 100% increase in the drying rate in comparison to convection-only trials. The results obtained in these studies are comparable with drying behaviors observed in electromagnetic assisted drying for bioproduct applications [Grassmann 1980, Ahrens et al 2003, Awuah et al 2005]. In the RF+Base case trials performed in this study, the contact temperatures were maintained at 150°C, and the convection temperatures were at 100°C. In the experimental setup, RF being situated between both conduction-enabled chambers, the application of the field was to ensure significant boosting of the pocket-based drying coupled with the increase in sample energy due to the contact cycles.
